01 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

Where AsyncRT fits

AsyncRT = Asynchronous Runtime. It is a native library for scheduling CPU work, representing future results, and managing host resources. A GPU inference still needs these CPU services. ↗ README.md:5

One selected host process in this view; named references connect clients to runtime services. Hardware and work items have different identities.

Concrete inputs and outputs

Objects in this guide: AR1 is a C++ CPUDevice; Q1 its WorkQueue; W0/W1 are OS worker threads; T1 is a movable closure; R1 is an AsyncValue allocation; C0 is an already-ready Chain value. These names are illustrative and persist across animation steps.

Storage: AR1, Q1, closures and AsyncValues live in host memory. GPU buffers and device code have separate device allocations. A worker issuing a CUDA call remains a CPU thread.

A small common runtime serves several clients

Algorithms submit work through an interface while runtime policy chooses threads, affinity and allocation. This makes compiler tasks, MAX model setup and Mojo continuations composable. A CPUDevice is a service owner, not a claim that inference arithmetic must run on the CPU. ↗ AsyncRTRuntime.md:10 ↗ CPUDevice.h:323

Three parts of the folder

Support/ holds chains, locations/diagnostics, queues, semaphores and affinity helpers. Runtime/ adds CPUDevice, AsyncValue, algorithms, allocation and scheduling. CompilerSupport/ adapts these services to LLVM/MLIR. Public interfaces are under include/; implementations are under lib/. docs/ explains intent, unittests/ records expected behavior, benchmarks/ measures individual mechanisms, and tools/ contains crash-report helpers. The complete file inventory below is clickable. ↗ README.md:11 ↗ README.md:23

Async has several meanings here

A C++ work item is a callable scheduled on host threads. An AsyncValue is a promise-like result location. A Mojo coroutine resume function can become a work item. A CUDA stream orders device commands. Python asyncio schedules Python coroutines. Their boundaries are connected by specific APIs; none of these words implies a network service or a new OS process. ↗ WorkQueue.h:67 ↗ AsyncRT.cpp:127 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2391

02 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

One process can contain many concurrent threads and tasks

“One host process” is the scope of a runtime diagram, not a limit on MAX Serve. Select the single-process view or the API/model-process boundary. The actual Serve startup also creates a telemetry consumer; these diagrams show only the relevant owners. ↗ model_worker.py:797↗ api_server.py:156

P0/PA/PM identify address spaces; W0/W1 identify OS threads; A1/B1/C1 identify work. Counts and interleavings are illustrative.

  3. Register C1 without blocking the caller

    R1 is pending. Registering a continuation stores a callback; it does not allocate an OS thread to sit and wait. The caller can proceed with other work.

    API · AsyncRTR1.andThenSync(C1) → andThen<false> → andThenOutOfLine(...)

    IN
    R1 is pending; C1 captures an owning R1 reference to read later.
    OUT
    C1 stored among R1’s waiters; registration returns without awaiting the payload.
    Thread / queue effect
    C1 is not runnable yet. No OS thread sits in the R1 waiters box.

  5. Construct 42 and publish readiness

    W0’s producer constructs R1’s payload and publishes Available atomically. Payload publication is data readiness, not an interprocess message.

    API · AsyncRTA1 returns 42 → emplaceAndDecRef<int>(42) → notifyReadyAndDecRef(kAvailable, ...)

    IN
    W0’s producer owns R1’s result reference; C1 is registered.
    OUT
    R1 payload=42; state atomically becomes Available; waiters detached.
    Thread / queue effect
    This finishes the dependency phase. It does not yet execute C1.

    Caller ancestry · current function in bold green

    Who calls emplace? The typed addTask wrapper, invoked by workItem.task() on W0. work() returns 42, then that wrapper publishes R1 on the same worker stack.

  6. Make the dependent closure runnable

    A waiter registered while pending is released through runWaiterLater. From the owning worker, addLocalTask puts C1 into that worker’s local list; a foreign caller falls back to shared dispatch.

    API · AsyncRTnotifyReadyAndDecRef → runWaiterLater(C1, Q1) → addLocalTask → W0.localTaskList.emplace_back(C1)

    IN
    R1 is ready; completing thread W0 belongs to Q1.
    OUT
    C1 is runnable on W0’s local callback list.
    Thread / queue effect
    The Q1 shared-queue fallback is skipped because getOwningWorkQueueThread() returned W0.

    Caller ancestry · current function in bold green

    OUT

    This illustrated ordering needs only W0/W1. A callback is work, not a new thread.

Concrete inputs and outputs

When can same-process concurrency happen?

Model initialization: Engine::Context::initModel queues single-model setup with addTask; the multi-model path uses andThenAsync. A runtime worker executes initialization while the caller follows its API’s wait policy. The source explicitly requires AsyncRT CPUDevice TLS for downstream buffer operations. ↗ EngineContext.cpp:294↗ EngineContext.cpp:297

Compilation: LLVMThreadPool::asyncEnqueue queues tasks in the CPUDevice WorkQueue and tracks a task group. Multiple independent native tasks can be in flight inside that compiler process. W0/W1 in the animation illustrate this possibility; not every graph or phase runs two tasks concurrently. ↗ LLVMThreadPool.cpp:50↗ LLVMThreadPool.cpp:64

A dependent continuation: one worker produces R1=42 while another performs independent work. C1 waits as a stored callable, then becomes runnable when R1 is published. This requires no separate process and no waiting thread per result. ↗ Algorithms.h:321↗ AsyncValue.h:176

GPU inference: a host routine submits a GPU command; device execution can overlap other host work permitted by dependencies. A stream wait can order GPU commands without putting the CPU into a blocking stream synchronize call. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1364↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1386

Can the standalone example also start another process?

Yes. When Graph receives kernels/ as a source package, package preparation runs mojo precompile through subprocess.run. That temporary compiler process produces P1 on disk; it is separate from the persistent Python host process and its AsyncRT worker threads. The single-process animation zooms into native runtime scheduling after that boundary, not the complete build/run process tree. ↗ paths.py:178↗ run.py:74

Two independent test processes can also prepare the same package path. The source uses process-specific staging and atomic os.replace to avoid a partially published .mojoc. This is a filesystem coordination case across processes, unlike two threads publishing an AsyncValue in shared host memory. ↗ paths.py:165↗ paths.py:179

The pools are not interchangeable

Q1 belongs to one selected native runtime. A process can have more runtime/queue instances, including NUMA partitions. A foreign thread means a thread not owned by this particular queue—even a worker from another queue can be foreign. “Model worker” is a Serve process; “response_worker” is a Python coroutine; “WorkQueueThread” is a native OS thread. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:929↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1339↗ zmq_interface.py:247

R1 waiters → W0 local callbacks: why not Q1?

First decide WHEN C1 may run; then decide WHERE it runs. R1 is an eventual integer; C1 is the consumer callable in this example. The three boxes represent different states of work, not three threads.

Diagram labelMeaning and owner
R1 waitersC1 is waiting for data

Callbacks retained by R1 while it is pending. The first can use R1’s unused payload area; additional callbacks use waiter-list nodes. No OS thread is parked in this box. ↗ AsyncValue.cpp:278

W0 local callbacksC1 is ready to execute

WorkQueueThread W0 owns localTaskList, a list of runnable WorkItems. W0 drains it in its runItems loop before checking affinity and shared tasks. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:422↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:601

Q1 · shared run queueIndependent work is ready to execute

Q1’s shared taskList accepts ordinary addTask submissions for eligible workers. It does not automatically inspect the values captured by a closure or wait for them. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1125↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:642

Example: C1 must read 42 after A1 produces it

// Illustrative C++; AR1 and consume are provided by the client.
// Selected animation schedule: A1 does not finish before registration.
auto R1 = AsyncRT::addTask(AR1, [] { return 20 + 22; });  // A1
R1.andThenSync([r = R1.copy()] {                        // C1
  if (r.isError()) return;  // application handles failure here
  consume(r.get());        // successful path sees 42
});
// Caller can continue: andThenSync did not await the pending payload.

Watch the existing comparisons:

Why not submit C1 to Q1 immediately?

Q1.addTask(C1) schedules a callable; it has no R1 dependency argument. A worker could pick C1 before A1 has produced 42. The application would then need its own wait/dependency handling before reading R1. Registering on R1 expresses the dependency directly and leaves workers free for runnable tasks. ↗ WorkQueue.h:141↗ AsyncValue.h:200

Why use W0’s local list after R1 is ready?

The pending andThenSync route tries to run the callback on the triggering worker. addLocalTask can append directly when that thread belongs to Q1; this skips a shared-queue handoff. Deferring C1 until the worker loop also avoids recursively invoking all dependent work inside A1’s publication call. The code implements these choices; the diagram makes no throughput or latency claim. ↗ AsyncValue.h:169↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:419

R1 waiters and Q1 are not competing destinations at registration. R1 stores a dependency; once it is satisfied, dispatch chooses a runnable-work destination. Callback registration can race with publication, so the implementation also handles readiness discovered during registration. The animation deliberately selects a pending-registration, W0-completion ordering. ↗ AsyncValue.cpp:329

A queue stores work; a thread executes it

Threads in one process share host objects, so a task can capture a reference to R1. Correct publication, locks and atomics coordinate their accesses. A semaphore post wakes a sleeping thread; it does not carry R1’s payload. Across PA/PM, the explicit ZeroMQ message boundary performs communication instead. ↗ Algorithms.h:326↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:955↗ zmq_interface.py:250

Why so many meanings of wait?

Python await: a coroutine suspends when its awaited operation is pending; the event-loop thread can run another coroutine. No new worker thread is created by await itself. ↗ zmq_interface.py:186

AsyncRT continuation: registering on a pending value returns without waiting for its payload. andThenSync may invoke immediately if already ready; andThenAsync explicitly queues an independent task. “Sync” does not mean this method blocks until a pending value completes. ↗ AsyncValue.h:772↗ AsyncValue.cpp:480

Native await by an owning worker: the calling function waits for its values, but the worker can execute other Q1 tasks in runItemsOnOwningThread. This is helping the queue, not Python asyncio. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1264

Native await by a foreign thread: register callbacks, then sleep on a private semaphore. The last completion decrements numRemaining to zero and posts the semaphore. Other Q1 workers produce the awaited values. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1282↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1300

Idle worker: no runnable work → publish suspended state → recheck queues → sema.wait. Enqueuing work posts a worker semaphore. This wake only means “look for work”; it is not completion of that work. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:735↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1165

GPU dependency vs host wait: cuStreamWaitEvent orders later commands on a GPU stream. cuStreamSynchronize waits on the calling host thread. cuEventQuery checks event status. A CPU task’s return, native result readiness, GPU completion and a Serve response are separate milestones. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1391↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2391↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:1245

Why use separate Serve processes as well?

The source gives PA and PM separate startup, readiness and IPC boundaries: PA awaits a process-ready event and channel connectivity; PM owns its pipeline lifecycle. Inside either address space, threads handle work without requiring a new process for each task. This describes the selected two-process slice, not a fixed total deployment process count. ↗ model_worker.py:815↗ model_worker.py:827

Concrete inputs and outputs

Actual constructor request: CPUDeviceOptions().withMainWillNotDonate(), allowUsingExistingOptions=true. Defaults include numThreads=0 (automatic), numaPartitioned=false and threadBusyWaitTime=200 µs unless overridden by the environment. The function-level thread-pool defaults and older design prose may differ; this route passes CPUDeviceOptions explicitly. ↗ CPUDevice.h:129

Illustrative output: DCPU.cpuDevice → AR1; AR1.workQueue → Q1; AR1.readyChain → C0; DCPU.streamChain → C0. This creates references and host services, not a user tensor.

Why CPU services exist when inference uses a GPU

Host routines still allocate metadata, schedule model initialization, track future results and invoke the device driver. AR1 supplies those services. The session retains CPU services alongside the accelerator contexts. ↗ EngineContext.cpp:294 ↗ CPUDevice.h:323

Why reuse a process-global owner

Several MAX/Mojo clients can share workers and allocation policy instead of each starting a private pool. The creation mutex makes a concurrent first-use race produce one global owner. Reuse normally checks option compatibility; this CpuDeviceContext explicitly permits existing options. It does not retroactively change an existing runtime to mainWillDonate=false. ↗ HostSystem.cpp:32 ↗ CpuDeviceContext.cpp:255

TLS and globals answer different questions

The global pointer finds the shared service. Thread-local storage identifies the runtime associated with the current thread. getCurrentCPUDeviceOrNull first checks TLS, then falls back to the global pointer and caches it in TLS. WorkQueue also tracks thread identity to decide whether a caller is one of its workers; having a CPUDevice pointer alone does not make a foreign thread a worker. ↗ CPUDevice.cpp:56 ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1230

Why an already-ready token

An empty stream needs an initial dependency that is already satisfied. Reusing C0 avoids allocating a new completed AsyncValue for every such use. Later enqueued operations produce new pending chains; C0 itself stays ready. ↗ CPUDevice.h:357

T1 is a closure, not a thread. A small set of OS workers runs many such work items. An ordinary task, a local continuation and an affinity task use different queues. ↗ WorkQueue.h:82 ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1125

Concrete inputs and outputs

Input: a=20, b=22, taskId=-1. Immediate API result: AsyncValueRef<int> pointing at R1. Later payload: 42. TaskFunction is llvm::unique_function<void()>; the typed addTask overload wraps a returning function in a void closure that fulfills R1. WorkItem is move-only. ↗ WorkQueue.h:67 ↗ Algorithms.h:321

Queue vocabulary: MPMC means multiple producers and multiple consumers. The shared queue accepts work from many submitting threads and is consumed by many workers. Local lists are owned by their worker; affinity rings route to a selected worker; overflow/spill lists handle enqueue pressure.

Small tasks amortize OS-thread cost

Reusing workers avoids creating an OS thread for each arithmetic operation or continuation. A submitted work item carries only the function and its captures, plus optional instrumentation. Keep work items short and avoid blocking I/O inside the pool. ↗ WorkQueue.h:82 ↗ WorkQueueNonblocking.md:88

Different queues preserve different intent

Local callbacks favor cheap same-thread continuation work. Affinity queues support a chosen worker and cache/device locality. Shared work can be picked up by any worker. The overflow path trades uncommon locking for reliable deferred enqueue; the source explicitly declines to guarantee fairness. This implementation should not be described as Tokio-style work stealing. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1200 ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1175

Deferred does not mean unfinished at return

The addTask contract forbids executing the task inline on the submitting call stack. Another worker may nevertheless complete it before addTask returns. Code must inspect readiness or register a continuation rather than assume a minimum delay. ↗ WorkQueue.h:132

05 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

A future value, its waiters, and publication

R1 is storage plus a readiness protocol. Consumers can register interest before its payload exists. Ready means either a value or an error; consumers must distinguish them. ↗ AsyncValue.h:161

Compare pending, already-ready, and foreign-thread completion. The same API name can take different dispatch paths.

Concrete inputs and outputs

Before: R1 holds no int; producer owns one reference; consumer retains another. After emplace(42): payload=42, Available state, producer reference consumed, queued consumer still keeps the value alive. get<int>() is valid only after checking the resolved type/state. ↗ AsyncValue.h:784

Four conceptual cases: pending; pending with waiters; ready value; ready error. The actual enum contains additional registration states used to coordinate concurrent construction. Indirect AsyncValues can later resolve to another AsyncValue; they are used when a result placeholder must be returned before its concrete value exists. ↗ AsyncValue.h:286 ↗ AsyncValue.cpp:548

Why registration races with completion

Thread A can register a consumer while thread B publishes the result. Both must agree whether the closure was linked into the waiter list or should be run using the ready path. Compare/exchange, atomic state changes and waiter-initialization flags prevent lost notification and access to half-initialized waiter storage. This synchronizes the readiness protocol; it does not make arbitrary writes to a mutable payload safe. ↗ AsyncValue.cpp:239 ↗ AsyncValue.cpp:360

Why pending sync callbacks use the local queue

A long chain of completions could otherwise recursively call consumer after consumer on one C++ stack. runWaiterLater keeps pending continuations near the triggering worker while deferring their invocation until the queue loop. The already-ready registration fast path can run immediately because its closure was just constructed at that call site. The animation follows implementation rather than the shorter descriptions in older AsyncValue prose. ↗ AsyncValue.h:521 ↗ AsyncValue.h:509

Why capture ownership explicitly

A raw waiter need not keep the AsyncValue alive. If the callback accesses R1, retain a reference or use the consuming-waiter wrapper. Otherwise producer-reference release may destroy R1 before the queued callback runs. Copying a reference retains the same object; it does not copy a tensor payload. ↗ AsyncValue.h:163 ↗ AsyncValueRef.h:125

Concrete inputs and outputs

Ordered stream: C0 ready → copy task produces C1 → compute task produces C2 → free task produces C3. The chains hold no matrix values. They encode “this side effect has happened.”

Fan-in: A ready and B pending means C must wait. When B becomes ready, exactly one final handler can run. If B is an error, the handler must forward the error instead of calling B.get().

ForkJoin sentinel: start=1; fork two tasks → 3; one task finishes → 2; join() removes the launch-side sentinel → 1; final task finishes → 0 and signals done. Here “fork” is a task API, not Linux fork() and not a child process.

Data and control use one readiness mechanism

Typed AsyncValues carry computed data; AsyncValue<Chain> carries only an ordering condition. Both can be composed with callbacks and fan-in. A graph’s ordering dependencies therefore need no separate blocked thread for each edge. The meaning of a ready chain comes from its producer: a host-submission chain must not be silently interpreted as GPU completion. ↗ Chain.h:23 ↗ CpuDeviceContext.cpp:297

Atomic counters coordinate independent completions

A and B can finish on different workers. The final decrement must run the completion function once. The shared heap state also retains the input references until that function returns. Readiness joins do not automatically implement error policy; the closure must check each input. ↗ Algorithms.h:79 ↗ Algorithms.h:109

Why ForkJoin starts at one

Tasks may finish while the caller is still adding more tasks. The extra launch-side count keeps done pending during that interval. join() removes it only after submission is complete. Without this sentinel, a fast first task could make the counter zero before the next task was launched. Keep the ForkJoin object alive through join(), since worker closures capture this. ↗ ForkJoin.h:66 ↗ ForkJoin.h:41

07 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

What await does to the calling thread

An owning worker can keep the pool progressing while it waits. A foreign caller uses a semaphore and lets the pool do the work. The CPU() cold path requests mainWillDonate=false, so its Python caller is normally in the foreign-thread category. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1221 ↗ CpuDeviceContext.cpp:254

Concrete inputs and outputs

Two workers, both doing blocking I/O: neither is available to execute a queued task that would satisfy them. This is the starvation risk behind the nonblocking-work policy.

Worker donation: W0 runs a task that awaits R1; it enters the queue loop and may execute R1’s producer, then return to its original call stack. The submitted task’s stack remains live during that nested wait.

Foreign caller: a Python thread waits for model initialization while W0/W1 run setup. No Python coroutine switching is implied. A CPUDevice TLS pointer and ownership of a WorkQueueThread are separate facts.

Avoid consuming the worker pool with passive waits

Finite pools can starve if every worker blocks waiting for queued work. Continuations express dependencies without holding a thread. When a synchronous API really needs to wait, an owning worker can donate execution to the queue. Blocking external I/O should be kept outside these work items and report completion back asynchronously. ↗ WorkQueueNonblocking.md:48 ↗ WorkQueue.h:158

Foreign threads retain their role

This implementation does not turn arbitrary threads into temporary Q1 workers. A foreign caller registers completion callbacks and waits on a private semaphore. The owning worker/main path uses the worker’s own semaphore so both new work and awaited-value completion can wake it. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1282 ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1259

Readiness is narrower than global quiescence

Other waiters attached to the same value can still be pending when await returns. If you need a later callback to finish, await a value or chain that the callback itself fulfills. Queue shutdown is a separate lifecycle operation. ↗ WorkQueue.h:169

08 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

Preventing the “queued work, sleeping workers” race

An idle worker must conserve CPU without missing newly queued work. AsyncRT coordinates queue publication, suspended bits and a semaphore. This is a concrete concurrency protocol, not periodic polling alone. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:735

Two valid interleavings show why a worker announces sleep before rechecking the queues.

Concrete inputs and outputs

Bad ordering to avoid: W0 sees “queue empty”; P enqueues T1 but sees “W0 awake”; W0 goes to sleep. T1 could remain stranded.

Actual ordering: W0 first publishes its suspended bit, fences and rechecks queues. P first publishes T1, fences and checks suspended bits. The source describes this as a Dekker handshake: one side must see the other’s publication. The scene illustrates this ordering, not a measured CPU memory trace.

Semaphore vs task: the task closure remains in the queue. The semaphore is a wake-up counter used to coordinate a sleeping thread. POSIX calls are shown; exact libc/kernel implementation details are outside this source boundary.

Sleep is a concurrency transition

Checking “empty” and then sleeping is not an atomic operation. Producers may arrive between those actions. The paired fences and suspended-bit protocol close that gap. Queue operations alone are insufficient for the documented cross-variable ordering, and the source records a hang caused by weakening it. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:735

A failed dequeue can be misleading

The shared queue may report dequeue failure while another worker has an optimistic claim in progress. The final idle path also checks approximate size and retries, with stop predicates for completed awaits or shutdown. Approximate size is not permission to read an item; it is a reason to avoid sleeping too early. ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:795

Balance wake latency and idle CPU

Spinning briefly can avoid repeated sleep/wake overhead under a burst of tasks; sleeping after the budget releases CPU capacity. This CPUDeviceOptions path defaults to 200 µs and honors MODULAR_THREAD_BUSY_WAIT_US. No animation duration represents that measured delay. ↗ CPUDevice.h:123 ↗ CPUDevice.h:129

AsyncRT drives the host side of GPU inference

AR1 schedules model setup and generated host work. CUDA owns device submission and completion semantics. Keep the CPU task, its result wrapper and the GPU command separate. ↗ EngineContext.cpp:289 ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:176

Concrete inputs and outputs

Actual attention buffers: Q/K/V are 32×32 float32, each 4096 bytes. AsyncValue payloads hold native values/wrappers around storage; an AsyncValue<Chain> does not hold those 4096 bytes.

Three clocks: H1 can return on the CPU; O’s native result wrapper can become ready; GPU0 can finish writing O later. A stream/event dependency provides the appropriate device ordering. The additional O_host readback in the animation is not part of the example’s printed Buffer list.

Local offload: CUDA user-space calls and the kernel driver coordinate device work. These are not MAX Serve HTTP requests, and a host WorkItem is not serialized to a remote worker. This page stops at the verified CUDA API boundary for private driver/hardware scheduling.

Setup needs runtime context on its worker

Engine::Context::initModel uses addTask for a single model; the multi-model path uses andThenAsync. Its source says downstream MGP_RT_BufferBorrowV2 requires the current AsyncRT CPUDevice in thread-local storage. The queue supplies that environment while retaining result and weight references. ↗ EngineContext.cpp:294 ↗ EngineContext.cpp:315

Host dispatch can be inline

AsyncRT does not require a queue hop for every function. The MGP primitive runs async kernels out of line; synchronous kernels can run inline when worker affinity permits. For the scheduled branch it captures operands/results, calls H1, then publishes indirect results after releasing context-reachable captures. This protects lifetime/order without equating host completion to GPU completion. ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:202 ↗ MGPPrimitives.cpp:220

Streams preserve device ordering

CUDA queues kernel/copy commands on a stream. Events or synchronization establish when preceding work has completed. AsyncRT’s CPU queue schedules host code that issues those commands; its worker IDs do not represent GPU blocks or CUDA streams. Refer to the NVIDIA research links below for stream diagrams; the pinned MAX sources establish the actual API call sites. ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2407 ↗ CUDADeviceContext.cpp:2391

Concrete inputs and outputs

Mojo bridge values (illustrative): resume=function pointer R, hdl=frame F1, desiredWorkerId=-1. The queued closure keeps R and F1’s handle; executing it calls R(F1).

LLVM task group: counter=1 sentinel; enqueue A/B → 3; task A completes → 2; wait releases sentinel → 1; task B completes → 0 and makes the chain ready.

Timeout: “wait up to 10 ms for C1” creates a deadline chain and a winner chain. A false timeout result does not terminate or cancel C1’s producer. TimerHeap.cancel removes a deadline notification, not arbitrary model work.

Shared scheduling, different language semantics

CompilerRT bridges carry ABI-stable pointers and handles. AsyncRT only needs the callable work item; it does not need to understand Python bytecode, the Mojo source syntax or the LLVM task’s compiler algorithm. Front ends retain their own state and express completion through chains/results. ↗ AsyncRT.cpp:127 ↗ LLVMThreadPool.cpp:64

Front-end async is not automatically the same API

Python asyncio uses coroutine/task scheduling in its event loop. The C++ AsyncRT await call synchronously waits for readiness using its queue/threads. The Mojo bridge schedules resume(handle) as native work. See the linked Python and Tokio documentation for comparison; this checkout’s code establishes AsyncRT behavior. ↗ Algorithms.h:38 ↗ AsyncRT.cpp:127

Timers need their own producer

TimerHeap maintains deadlines using a dedicated thread, a mutex and a condition variable. Expiration fulfills an AsyncValue<Chain>, bringing the timed event back into the normal readiness system. The timeout bridge arbitrates done versus expired with an atomic flag so it fulfills its winner chain only once. Do not confuse this mechanism with cancellation of a running task. ↗ TimerHeap.cpp:60 ↗ AsyncRT.cpp:99

11 / ASYNCHRONOUS RUNTIME

Who owns memory, and when can the runtime stop?

References let asynchronous work outlive the function that submitted it. Retaining a wrapper, retaining its storage and retaining AR1 are different ownership relationships. ↗ CPUDevice.h:323 ↗ AsyncValue.h:741

Standalone native-owner teardown. Python CPU caching can retain AR1 for process lifetime; counts here are illustrative.

Concrete inputs and outputs

Result lifetime: caller owns ref(R1); task captures another ref(R1). Returning from the submit function does not destroy R1. Task completion consumes its producer ref; the caller’s ref still keeps the result alive.

Runtime lifetime: AsyncValue stores a compact runtime identity used to reach allocation/scheduling services. Keep AR1 alive through its real owners while values and work need it. Do not treat that compact ID as a strong CPUDeviceRef.

NUMA example: global AR1 can own partition AR-N0 and AR-N1, each with its own allocator, workers and compact identity. A delegate queue routes to partition queues. Memory locality and device-affinity choices are policy; no particular physical CPU count is assumed here.

Keep allocation policy independent of algorithms

The allocator interface accepts byte size/alignment and supports different underlying policies. Debug wrappers can track leaks or allocations. CPUDeviceOptions chooses the allocator; tensor-heavy data can follow the runtime’s placement policy, while tiny ordinary C++ allocations need not all use this interface. ↗ AsyncRTRuntime.md:141 ↗ CPUDevice.cpp:156

The Python CPU cache can retain the runtime for process lifetime

The Python CPU cache deliberately keeps owning references until process exit. Closing one session is therefore not a promise that AR1’s destructor runs. This animation teaches the native teardown contract when final ownership does end, rather than claiming the fused_attention.py run executes every teardown step. ↗ Device.cpp:648

Drain work while services are still valid

CPUDevice::~CPUDevice explicitly shuts down the queue first because outstanding work may still need AR1 or enqueue follow-on work. Shutdown is not a cancellation request for arbitrary producers outside the queue. Clients must honor lifetime and shutdown contracts and ensure external work is settled. Joining workers precedes invalidating runtime identity. ↗ CPUDevice.cpp:118 ↗ ThreadPoolWorkQueue.cpp:1080

NUMA is a separate configuration branch

The partitioned route creates a CPUDevice and thread pool per NUMA node, then a top-level delegate queue. Keeping execution and host data close can reduce cross-socket traffic. That branch is optional and defaults off in CPUDeviceOptions; it is not implied merely by Accelerator(0). ↗ HostSystem.cpp:54 ↗ CPUDevice.h:146

Where to inspect a problem

For a stranded task, inspect queue routing, suspended state and the producer of its dependencies. For a never-ready value, inspect producer reference ownership and success/error publication. For unexpected inline execution, check the already-ready andThenSync path or MGP sync branch. For a wrong worker, inspect taskId, WorkQueue ownership and CPUDevice TLS separately. The folder inventory includes unit tests and benchmarks as reading references; this walkthrough has not executed MAX or measured GPU behavior. ↗ WorkQueueTest.cpp:60 ↗ AsyncValueTest.cpp:49

Object or APIMeaning and implementation
CPUDevice / AR1Native owner of allocator, WorkQueue and ready chain. One instance can support many tasks. ↗ CPUDevice.h:323

Chain / C0Empty marker type; an AsyncValue<Chain> is an ordering/completion signal chosen by its producer. ↗ Chain.h:23

ForkJoinTracks a dynamically submitted set of tasks with an atomic counter and completion chain. It does not create processes. ↗ ForkJoin.h:34

RESEARCH → VISUAL DESIGN

Further reading and animation choices

The diagrams were built for the pinned MAX implementation. The following primary sources informed the comparisons and visual techniques.

  • Modular · AsyncRT source and design documents

    Implementation authority is the pinned local source linked throughout this page. Public design documents help explain the library’s purpose; where older prose differs, this reader follows the actual source.

  • TensorFlow · TFRT Host Runtime Design

    Design inspiration: draw future values and readiness dependencies independently of worker threads. This is a comparison, not a claim that MAX uses TFRT.

  • TensorFlow blog · TFRT: A Progress Update (2022)

    Design inspiration: asynchronous work has costs; fast synchronous paths matter too. Applied here as explicit already-ready and inline-vs-queued branches, using MAX’s own conditions.

  • Tokio blog · Making the Tokio scheduler 10x faster (2019)

    The article’s Scheduling loop, Single queue, Sharded and Message passing drawings inspired these original interactive diagrams: task tiles, queue cells, CPU worker boxes and explicit arrows. AsyncRT’s source determines dispatch; Tokio’s work stealing is not copied.

  • NVIDIA blog · How to Overlap Data Transfers in CUDA C/C++

    Visual inspiration: separate host progress from ordered device-stream commands and show copy/compute completion. Actual overlap depends on hardware, streams and memory-transfer conditions.

  • NVIDIA · CUDA asynchronous execution

    API background for separate submission and completion milestones, streams and events. The local MAX call tree links the actual Driver API implementations.

  • Python · Coroutines and Tasks

    Comparison boundary: Python await/coroutines and event-loop tasks are language-level APIs; C++ AsyncRT await and native work items have the distinct behavior shown in this reader.
